With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.

Cryptography and Security.title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

Cryptography and Security.title: TrackShield: An Efficient Runtime Defense Against Availability Attacks on High-Performance Real-Time Multi-Object Tracking
Cryptography and Security.summary: High-performance camera-based perception pipelines must sustain per-frame real-time budgets on resource-constrained embedded GPU platforms. Availability attacks such as SlowTrack inflate the persistent state of multi-object trackers: data-association workload accumulates across frames, so per-frame latency increases and drives the pipeline past its deadline. Detector- and NMS-layer defenses do not directly control this persistent tracker-side resource. We present TrackShield, a lightweight runtime resource-management layer that protects the tracker at the point where attack-induced workload accumulates. TrackShield combines low-overhead anomaly monitoring with staged birth capping, pruning of young or weakly matched tracks, and per-stage association-input admission control. Its hard admission guard provides a deterministic bound on admitted association workload, independently of the heuristic monitor. On a Jetson AGX Orin, TrackShield reduces attacked tracking-stage latency from $139.90$ to $6.27$\,ms and whole-pipeline P99 latency from $190.9$ to $48.8$\,ms, at a benign MOTA cost of $1.06$ points. As an availability defense, TrackShield focuses on keeping the tracker responsive under attack instead of recovering the full tracking accuracy degraded by adversarial detections.

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Maliciousness: Static and Runtime Attack-Surface Profiling of Agent Skills
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agent skills are Markdown documents that a tool-using agent reads as instructions and then acts on with the privileges of the session that loaded them. Installing one grants authority (the standing to direct the agent, not new privilege), and the size of that grant is what we measure. We present a two-phase attack-surface profiling methodology that combines whole-bundle static analysis and dependency provenance checking with instrumented sandbox execution and separate model-based assessment of the resulting traces. We apply the methodology to 6,309 listings from two marketplaces, selecting listings for execution without conditioning that decision on a prior threat or risk signal. Half the corpus carries evidence of shell-execution capability; the corresponding shares are 35% for filesystem read, 31% each for filesystem write and network egress, and 13% for credential access; seven listings in ten carry at least one elevated capability. That is the surface a user accepts at install time, and almost none of it is visible then. A permission model exists but is close to inert. Authors may list the tools a skill pre-approves in its own frontmatter, which removes confirmation prompts rather than restricting what the skill can reach; of the 6,061 listings whose frontmatter parses, 770 declare anything at all, the vocabulary cannot express credential or environment access, and nothing checks what it does express against the bundle. Declaring is also not declaring accurately: 59% of declaring listings understate what their bundle can do. ClawHub declares roughly twice as often as skillsmp, yet under-declares on 88% of its declarations against 31%. Triage at the marketplace boundary therefore cannot rest on what a listing declares. It must rest on what the bundle can do. These results position capability-oriented attack-surface profiling as a necessary complement to maliciousness detection.
Cryptography and Security.comment: This paper has 13 pages, 9 figures, and 3 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: It's My Agent, Not Me: Personal Privacy Boundaries in AI-Delegated Information Sharing
Cryptography and Security.summary: Aligning AI systems with human privacy preferences requires understanding individuals' nuanced disclosure behaviors beyond general privacy norms. Yet eliciting these boundaries remains challenging because they involve context-dependent trade-offs. We present an elicitation approach that probes individuals' privacy boundaries through a discriminative task. Through a between-subjects study with varying communication roles and delegation conditions, we collected 1,650 privacy boundaries from 169 participants across 60 scenarios. We examined how communication roles, AI delegation, and individual differences influence boundaries. Results show that communication roles significantly influence sensitivity to disclosure granularity or identifiability, depending on whose private information is shared; AI delegation and individuals' need for privacy heighten sensitivity to disclosed identifiers. Our analysis further reveals how AI delegation shifts privacy preferences across contexts, highlighting new complexities in AI-mediated communication. We advocate eliciting nuanced privacy boundaries within real-world data flows by considering roles and AI delegation, and enabling user involvement in guiding privacy-aware AI behavior.

Cryptography and Security.title: Majority Bit-Aware Watermarking For Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: The growing deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised concerns about their misuse in generating harmful or deceptive content. To address this issue, watermarking methods have been proposed to embed identifiable multi-bit messages into generated text for misuse tracing. However, existing methods often suffer from a fundamental trade-off between text quality and decoding accuracy. In particular, they have to restrict the size of the preferred token set (i.e., green list) during encoding to maintain a detectable watermark signal for decoding, which inevitably degrades generation quality. To improve this trade-off, we propose a novel message encoding paradigm called \textit{majority bit-aware encoding}, which relaxes the watermark signal strength from the green list size. This strategy allows for a strong watermark signal to be preserved in generated texts even when using a large green list. We introduce two instantiations of this paradigm: MajorMark and MajorMark$^{+}$, where the latter is specifically optimized for long messages. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that our methods achieve higher decoding accuracy and superior text quality compared to prior baselines. The code is at https://github.com/JiiahaoXU/MajorMark.
Cryptography and Security.comment: This work has been accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: A2ABreak: Systematic Security Analysis of the A2A Protocol
Cryptography and Security.summary: The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation, is an open standard that enables autonomous AI agents to discover, authenticate with, and delegate tasks to one another across organizational boundaries. Designed to complement the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool integration, A2A is rapidly emerging as the horizontal communication layer of the multi-agent ecosystem. Yet the protocol's security has received no systematic analysis. This paper presents A2ABreak, the first rigorous systematic security analysis of the A2A protocol. We introduce a novel framework that utilizes an LLM-assisted extraction of a verified finite-state machine directly from the natural-language specification, producing a unified model of 37 states and 76 transitions from 929 formalized statements, and then systematically reasons over this model to discover protocol-level vulnerabilities through adversarial verification, under a full-compliance assumption. Our analysis uncovers 11 new vulnerabilities, each exploitable by a specification-compliant adversary without requiring any implementation flaw. Among the findings are cross-client context injection through unprotected context identifiers, credential harvesting via multi-hop identity loss in delegation chains, and data exfiltration through rogue agents advertising unattested capability claims. A2ABreak achieves 73.3% precision and 84.6% F1 against manual expert review, while a zero-shot LLM baseline operating over the same specification produces zero confirmed findings, demonstrating that explicit formal grounding is essential for sound protocol security analysis.

Cryptography and Security.title: AgentCIScope: Grounded Contextual Integrity Evaluation for LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM agents are becoming increasingly capable of handling daily workspace tasks by interacting with application environments through tool calls. However, as agents read and write sensitive user data across email, documents, and other applications, a central privacy question is whether they preserve contextual integrity (CI), that is, whether the information flows they produce comply with context-specific disclosure constraints. Existing work either focuses on model-level privacy leakage or evaluates agents in limited application environments with manually constructed disclosure constraints. In this work, we introduce AgentCIScope, a unified platform and benchmark for evaluating agent-level contextual integrity through executable, multi-step tasks across diverse, realistic application environments. AgentCIScope transforms public and synthetic privacy cases into executable agent tasks, with disclosure constraints grounded in three criteria: governing privacy policies, persona-based agreement, and a predefined sensitive-attribute taxonomy. Based on AgentCIScope, we evaluate 12 agents on 936 tasks and find that strong task-completion capability does not guarantee contextual-integrity preservation: single-run leakage rates range from 32.5% to 94.4%, while repeating each task five times further increases leakage by 4-19 percentage points. Leakage varies substantially across attributes: personal preferences and booking details have average leakage rates of 84.7% and 76.5%, compared with 17.1% for credit-card information and 29.4% for SSNs; environments: calendar has the highest average leakage rate as an information source, while WhatsApp ranks highest as an information destination; and governing privacy policies. AgentCIScope provides deep insights into agent privacy leakage and serves as a unified testbed for developing privacy-preserving agents.

Cryptography and Security.title: Towards Tackling Application Logic Flaws through Autonomous Formal-Logic Modeling and Automated Reasoning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Logic flaws pose significant challenges in the design and implementation of modern, semantically rich systems and applications, impacting security, privacy, and trust. These flaws are inherently tied to business-specific semantics and threat models, making their discovery and reasoning difficult and hard to scale. Real-world systems often exhibit diverse application features, complex protocol logic, and domain-specific threat models, necessitating substantial human effort and domain expertise for effective security analysis. In this paper, we introduce LL-Verifier, a novel, automated framework for identifying logic vulnerabilities built on (1) large language models for autonomous modeling, and (2) logic model checkers for rigorous reasoning. LL-Verifier processes natural language inputs, in particular protocol descriptions and security goals, to automatically generate formal logic models and properties expressed in a new logic language built on a generic logic language Maude, optimized for modeling arbitrary application-level semantics. These formal models are then converted into logical state machines, enabling exhaustive, rigorous verification through logic level model checking. This approach streamlines the analysis of diverse, application-level protocols deployed in real-world scenarios, offering automated, exhaustive, and precise reasoning within their logical constraints. We evaluated the high effectiveness, efficiency, and practicality of LL-Verifier by applying it to 27 access control protocols of widely used IoT devices, which come with vendor-specific logic flows and semantics. While LL-verifier tackles a hard problem in application security, i.e., automatic logic flaws discovery, our analysis uncovers a range of sophisticated logic vulnerabilities in IoT protocols and devices with serious security and privacy implications.

Cryptography and Security.title: Cooking Up Risks: Benchmarking and Reducing Food Safety Risks in Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Food safety directly affects human health in daily life, as unsafe preparation or storage can lead to contamination and foodborne illness. PwC's 2025 consumer survey reports that 47% of respondents are comfortable using generative AI for meal planning, highlighting the need for safe food-related assistance. Yet the safety of large language models (LLMs) against malicious food-related requests remains underexplored. We introduce FoodGuardBench, an FDA-grounded benchmark with 2,124 seed malicious questions, 16,992 variants from eight jailbreak strategies, and 1,000 benign questions across five food-safety risk categories. Across twelve LLMs, the mean overall ASR is 25.51%, whereas the average per-model maximum across eight attacks is 60.59%, revealing that testing only one attack can substantially underestimate the full extent of food safety risk. For several models, nearly half or more of unsafe answers are rated as ready-to-use guides for harmful actions. Existing general-purpose guardrails average 96.25% benign utility but only 55.80% detection accuracy against these eight jailbreak attacks. Using FoodGuardBench, we fine-tune FoodGuard-4B, a food-safety-specific guardrail that achieves 97.64% out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy while maintaining high benign utility. This demonstrates the value of FoodGuardBench for identifying and mitigating food safety risks.

Cryptography and Security.title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments and Open Problems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) address the quantum threat from opposite directions: PQC replaces vulnerable public-key algorithms with schemes believed to resist quantum cryptanalysis, while QKD derives keys whose secrecy rests on physical assumptions rather than computational ones. Because each approach has a distinct failure mode, a growing body of work combines them so that a session key remains secure if either component holds. We first establish the deployed baseline, hybrid classical-plus-PQC key exchange, against which QKD-augmented designs must be judged. We then propose a taxonomy of hybrid PQC-QKD designs along eight dimensions (integration layer, combiner construction, authentication scope and source, QKD topology, trusted entities, key-delivery interface, classical component, and evidence type), and use it to compare published protocols, including Muckle and its successors, MACsec and TLS integrations, and IKEv2 mechanisms standardised in RFCs 8784, 9370, and 9867. We examine key-combiner constructions in light of the KEM-combiner literature and of NIST, ETSI, and ITU-T guidance, and map the security arguments for hybrid PQC-QKD protocols onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, established guarantee, and limitations. We synthesise deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks, distinguishing the few testbeds that have run PQC in the key path from pure-QKD deployments, and summarise the standards and policy landscape, including the positions of national security agencies that recommend against relying on QKD alone. We close with open problems: authentication of the QKD classical channel, shared-infrastructure threat models, device certification versus formal proofs, formal verification of hybrid handshakes, and the lack of peer-reviewed deployment economics.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 34 pages, 15 tables, 3 figures. Survey; submitted to ACM Computing Surveys

Cryptography and Security.title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
Cryptography and Security.summary: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.

Cryptography and Security.title: Limits of Statistical Assurance for Embodied and Agentic AI under Adaptive Adversaries
Cryptography and Security.summary: Finite safety assessments cannot exclude an adversary that preserves unattacked behavior until certification and activates afterward. We characterize this limitation for embodied and tool-use AI. An adversary that matches the complete observation law until observable, irrevocable certification and retains intervention access afterward attains $v\mathbb{E}[(n-S_0)_+]$ expected post-certification events over $n$ trials, where $v$ is the active event probability and $S_0$ the unattacked certification time. The result covers adaptive and privately randomized evaluators. Switching at certification is exactly optimal for a fixed likelihood-ratio test under memoryless, event-increasing interventions without a binding intervention budget. A positive clean-certification requirement forces linear worst-case expected excess when intervention raises event rates over an authorized deployment horizon, even if certification is deferred to the deadline. In simulated RoCo collaboration, switching yields commanded-separation violations in 34 of 36 post-certification episodes. Preregistered randomized AgentDojo trials estimate 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation (95% interval [1.67, 2.29]). An adversarial language-model controller infers hidden certification from noisy evaluation receipts and times intervention accordingly. With permanent revocation, a mixture likelihood-ratio monitor bounds cumulative excess above a prespecified reference rate at square-root order, up to logarithmic factors, on every sample path. A single fixed alternative can permit linear expected excess under stationary attacks. Against a controller observing the monitor's rule and statistic, live mixture monitoring reduces violations from 12.00 to 3.81 per 24 assigned task opportunities. Revocation also reduces tasks executed.

Cryptography and Security.title: Physical Layer Anomaly Detection via Adaptive Gaussian Mixture Model
Cryptography and Security.summary: Physical-layer spoofing attacks pose a critical threat to wireless localization systems by manipulating channel state information (CSI). Detecting such attacks becomes particularly challenging when the attacker and the legitimate node are spatially proximate, as their CSI characteristics become increasingly similar. To address this challenge in indoor scenarios, we propose an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM)-based detection framework that learns legitimate CSI patterns and detects spatial inconsistency through statistical anomaly detection. Using a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) experimental dataset with 64 uniform linear array (ULA) antenna and 5 mm spatial resolution, we evaluated our detector against CSI spoofing attacks with spatial displacements ranging from 50 mm to 450 mm. The adaptive GMM achieves 95-98% detection rate for displacements above 150 mm while maintaining 1% false alarm rate. We benchmark our approach against conventional GMM, local outlier factor (LOF), one-class support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) classifiers, demonstrating overall superior detection performance of our proposed classifier.

Cryptography and Security.title: An Initial Study of Physiological Markers for Deepfake Speech Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Conventional deepfake speech detectors primarily target synthesis artifacts and often degrade under unseen attacks or recording conditions. Human speech, however, contains physiological markers associated with respiration, phonation, and temporal coordination arising from the speech-production system that synthesizers may not reproduce faithfully. This motivates the hypothesis that deepfake speech can be detected by identifying inconsistencies in these patterns, which we test using 36 handcrafted physiological markers organized into respiratory, vocal, and temporal categories. We evaluate the marker vectors with logistic regression and SVM classifiers on pooled English recordings. The best in-domain system achieves a 21.40% equal error rate (EER), while logistic regression achieves 32.77% on the out-of-domain dataset pair. Since the markers describe specific speech-production properties, the logistic-regression coefficients indicate whether higher marker values push the classifier toward bona fide or deepfake speech. These results provide initial evidence that physiological markers offer a useful, interpretable signal for deepfake speech detection.

Cryptography and Security.title: Unmasking the Secret Code: Using Canaries to Show How Masked Context Controls Memorization in SFT
Cryptography and Security.summary: Canaries, or synthetic training records containing known secrets, are widely used to assess whether language models reveal information from their training data. But how much do these measurements depend on the canaries themselves? We study this question through controlled fine-tuning experiments with language and vision-language models, spanning synthetic tasks and tasks where training improves useful performance. Whether a secret is provided in the training input strongly changes what the model learns; for example, models can reproduce a secret in the input yet fail to recall it when it is removed, even after extensive repetition during training. When training instead requires predicting the secret from the surrounding context, later recall can become reliable. Repetition alone is therefore insufficient to characterize memorization. We also find that changing when a canary appears, or which other canaries accompany it, can substantially change measured memorization without increasing that canary's repetition count. These results show that canary measurements depend on how secrets are presented during training and tested afterward. Audits should test whether their conclusions hold across these choices before extending them to other training records.

Programming Languages.title: FlowBook: Enforcing Reproducibility in Computational Notebooks
Programming Languages.summary:
Computational notebooks interleave code cells with their outputs and let users edit and execute cells in arbitrary order. This flexibility supports interactive exploration, but it also allows outputs to become inconsistent with the notebook's current code and data. Such inconsistencies can lead users to draw invalid scientific conclusions. We argue that notebooks should always be output consistent: every output should match what a top-to-bottom execution of the current code would produce. Forcing a top-to-bottom execution after each edit would guarantee this, but at prohibitive cost: such an execution can take minutes to hours.
  We present FlowBook, a dynamic analysis for Python notebooks that enforces output consistency without giving up out-of-order execution. FlowBook does this by enforcing a stronger property, rerun consistency: no location read by a cell may be written by any cell below it. Rerun consistency guarantees that rerunning a cell later, in any order, reproduces its current output. FlowBook tracks each cell's read and write sets at cell boundaries, blocks updates that would violate rerun consistency, and marks as stale any cell whose inputs may have changed. We prove that a notebook with no stale cells is both rerun and output consistent. Users remain free to execute cells in arbitrary order; the only restriction is that recorded outputs may not silently depend on the order in which cells were executed.
  Across 61 real-world notebooks, FlowBook flagged 203 rerun-inconsistent cells. Rerunning 62% led to output inconsistencies. A further 21% change notebook state with no visible output, which can affect the results of later edits and reruns; only 5% are false positives of FlowBook's conservative analysis. FlowBook's AI repair agent repaired all 203 cells with local edits and no human intervention. FlowBook's median overhead is only 26 ms per cell execution.

Programming Languages.title: Soliduzz: Finding Miscompilations in Smart-Contract Compilers with Assertion-Driven Equivalence Oracles
Programming Languages.summary:
Smart contracts compiled to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) can manage high-value assets and are difficult to patch after deployment. Compiler miscompilations are therefore especially dangerous: compilation succeeds, but the generated bytecode does not preserve the semantics of the source program. Existing smart-contract compiler fuzzers either focus on robustness failures or rely on differential oracles that compare compiler configurations.
  We present Soliduzz, an approach for finding miscompilations in EVM smart-contract compilers using assertion-driven equivalence oracles. Soliduzz uses product programs to encode semantic equivalence as executable assertions. The key shift is to compile these self-checking programs and let off-the-shelf fuzzers and symbolic execution engines explore the resulting bytecode for assertion violations, without requiring compiler-specific support from the analyzer.
  Soliduzz instantiates this idea with two complementary families of metamorphic transformations. The first starts from equivalent expressions and lifts them into smart-contract code that deliberately exercises EVM-specific features such as storage, data locations, control flow, contract interactions, and inline assembly. The second generalizes Equivalence Modulo Inputs (EMI) from fixed concrete inputs to symbolic input spaces. Our symbolic EMI records coverage in the original computation and uses it to guard mutations in the transformed computation. Together, these transformations produce product programs that assert that paired computations yield the same outputs.
  We evaluate Soliduzz on three EVM smart-contract compilers (solc, solx, and vyper) using several analysis tools. Overall, Soliduzz exposes 29 bugs. Of these, 24 are compiler bugs: 6 miscompilations, 17 internal compiler errors, and 1 hang. The remaining 5 are bugs in the analysis tools.

Programming Languages.title: OpenMQPI: An MLIR-based Pipeline to Offload Quantum Circuits via OpenMP
Programming Languages.summary: Quantum computing introduces specialized software stacks and programming interfaces that are often tightly coupled to specific ecosystems and hardware backends, limiting interoperability and software reuse. For HPCQC application developers, this complicates the integration of quantum accelerators into existing applications. Existing quantum frameworks also use ecosystem-specific circuit representations and compilation pipelines, hindering integration with established heterogeneous compiler infrastructures. We propose OpenMQPI, an MLIR-based OpenMP extension for quantum programming that leverages OpenMP's standardized target offloading infrastructure to integrate quantum resources into HPC applications. OpenMQPI introduces QPIR, a lightweight MLIR dialect for representing quantum circuits within OpenMP target regions, and a compiler pipeline that performs quantum-specific optimizations and lowers circuits to executables compatible with OpenMP offloading. At runtime, an MQSS plugin enables the generated executable to offload quantum circuits to quantum hardware through the OpenMP target offloading model. We evaluate OpenMQPI using the VQE, QFT, and Deutsch-Jozsa algorithms with 5, 10, 15, and 20 qubits, comparing execution times against Qiskit and CUDA Quantum. OpenMQPI achieves the lowest average VQE execution time across all tested qubit configurations. At 20 qubits, it requires 5.18 s, compared with 5.83 s for Qiskit and 7.39 s for CUDA Quantum. For QFT and Deutsch-Jozsa, OpenMQPI achieves execution times comparable to Qiskit and lower than those of CUDA Quantum.

Programming Languages.title: From Rocq to Metal: A Pipeline for Formally Verified Microcontroller Firmware
Programming Languages.summary: Enforcing invariants in safety-critical firmware is increasingly urgent as generated code becomes widespread, but standard extraction targets for proof assistants require runtimes too large for many embedded devices. We present a pipeline for running formally verified Rocq firmware logic on Cortex-M microcontrollers. The pipeline extracts Gallina to Scheme, compiles it with Encore!, a bare-metal Continuation-Passing Style (CPS) bytecode virtual machine, and embeds the result in no_std Rust firmware. We structure applications as pure state-transition functions, so the business logic is proved in Rocq while the event/effect boundary, host callbacks, compiler, and VM remain explicit trusted components: no proof yet relates bytecode execution to Gallina semantics. On eight firmware workloads, from APDU parsing to a credential store, Encore! runs unmodified Rocq-extracted code within the 50 KiB RAM budget of ST33-class targets on every input size, where CertiRocq's generated code runs out of memory on the larger ones, at the price of up to 10 times more executed instructions than CertiRocq; a transaction-signing application is validated on physical Ledger Flex hardware.
Programming Languages.comment: Preprint: Accepted to the 19th International Conference on Verification and Evaluation of Computer and Communication Systems (VECoS 2026)

Programming Languages.title: Stdlib or Third-Party? Empirical Performance and Correctness of LLM-Assisted Zero-Dependency Python Libraries
Programming Languages.summary:
Third-party Python libraries introduce dependency-management overhead, supply-chain risk, and deployment friction. We study when eliminating a dependency preserves enough correctness and performance to justify the gains in footprint, deployability, and trust surface. Our testbed is zerodep, 44 single-file, stdlib-only Python modules spanning 12 categories, each benchmarked against its reference library.
  Three performance regimes emerge. Stdlib-only implementations achieve parity (within 2x) in the majority of cases; many outperform their references by 5x-115x where architectural overhead dominates; and a clear cliff appears for C-extension-backed computation (image processing, binary serialization, low-level crypto), confirmed by PyPy JIT and profiling experiments. Beyond speed, stdlib modules reduce installed footprint by orders of magnitude (median 31 KB vs. 700 KB), import 2.2x faster, and eliminate 88 transitive dependencies maintained by 128 distinct PyPI accounts.
  Analysis of the LLM-assisted development process across all 44 modules shows that specification completeness, not model capability, is a strong predictor of generation success, and that contract-linked review reduces review volume by 5x while eliminating compatibility regressions. Together, these results turn dependency elimination from an anecdotal coding style into an evidence-based engineering tradeoff.

Programming Languages.title: Compositional Information Geometry of Probabilistic Programs
Programming Languages.summary: We study the compositional, intensional information geometry of probabilistic programs. For a first-order probabilistic programming language with finite random variables, we construct a contravariant lax monoidal functor that, for a program of type $X \to Y$, pulls back a (degenerate) Riemannian metric on $Y$ to $X$. It specialises to the Fisher metric in the case of standard statistical models and to ordinary pullback in the case of deterministic programs. We further justify this construction in two ways. First, we show that this functor arises as a pullback of geometry from a universal space of programs over a type $Y$ with a fixed trace space. Second, we show that it is a special case of a more general pullback construction over weighted measures. Our compositional geometry depends on the presentation of the program, and we study how it relates to the (non-compositional) geometry of the realised measures by establishing a three-level inequality relating our score-velocity metric for the program, the program's corresponding output-conditioned metric, and the standard Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric of the realised family. Finally, we show how the theory can be extended to accommodate continuous random variables using diffeological quasi-Borel spaces. We also discuss several concrete directions for future work.

Programming Languages.title: QEDIA: Quantum Program Verification in Lean
Programming Languages.summary:
Practical quantum programs interleave quantum and classical computation: classical data shape the quantum operations that are performed, and measurement outcomes shape the classical computation that follows. Formal verification of such programs in a proof assistant requires mechanizing a program logic that handles this interplay consistently at every level, from the mathematics of quantum mechanics, through program syntax and semantics, to specifications and proof rules. Such mechanizations, along with the program proofs built on them, typically require substantial manual effort.
  We present QEDIA, a framework for verifying quantum programs with classical variables in Lean 4. At its foundation is an open library that formalizes the quantum Hoare logic QHL+ across all these levels and proves the logic sound for both partial and total correctness. We construct the library and the program proofs, under human supervision, using an LLM-based prover agent, whose general-purpose core we extend for quantum program verification. We illustrate QEDIA with verified programs including the quantum Fourier transform, phase estimation, repeat-until-success circuits, and Hamiltonian simulation.

Programming Languages.title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
Programming Languages.summary:
Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output. However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string. For example, most prompts contain both instructions ("Summarize this paper into a paragraph") and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks.
  This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM. This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security. This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting.
  We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases. We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.

Programming Languages.title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
Programming Languages.summary: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.

Software Engineering.title: PreciseCoder: Faithful and Generalizable Debugging Beyond Unit-Test Rewards
Software Engineering.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) from unit tests is the common recipe for post-training code models, but a unit test only asks whether the final program passes. We analyze what this unit-test-only reward teaches a model during debugging and find that, while it raises pass rates, it also teaches the model to edit more and to hallucinate bugs in code that is already correct. We introduce PreciseCoder, a training algorithm that augments the unit-test reward with a signal for semantically verified, localized edits, which correlates with smaller edits and higher pass rates. On 4B, 9B, and 27B models, PreciseCoder reduces the average number of edit lines from 7-15to 3 at a pass rate on par with unit-test-only training. Trained only on single-line bugs, PreciseCoder can generalize to repository-level program repair, where it resolves more issues with smaller patches. Its precision also transfers from weaker to stronger models: given the reasoning trace of a 9B PreciseCoder model, frontier models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Qwen3.8-Max gain 4.6-12.4 points in edit precision with no additional training. Linguistic analysis of the thinking traces shows that our reward encourages the model to reason about individual lines, name the buggy ones, and form consistent bug hypotheses.

Software Engineering.title: Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

Software Engineering.title: SolBehave: Evaluating the Behavioural Correctness of LLM-Generated Smart Contracts
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models increasingly generate Solidity smart contracts that, once deployed, can never be patched, making a single latent fault permanent and exploitable. Yet current evaluations mostly ask only whether generated code compiles. We introduce SolBehave, a benchmark for evaluating the correctness of model-generated contracts at scale, moving beyond ad hoc unit tests. Across 250 real, reproducible Ethereum contracts, we apply three complementary tests of behavioural fidelity: differential fuzzing, historical-transaction replay, and, as our core contribution, synthetic-transaction replay guided by a Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graph that enumerates the space of legitimate function-call sequences. Differential fuzzing compares each generated function with the original on automatically generated inputs; historical replay compares the whole contract on the transactions it actually received on-chain; DCR-guided replay compares it on sequences of calls that follow its intended usage, including orderings that never occurred on-chain. We evaluate seven state-of-the-art open-weight models after one round of automated repair. Compilation success ranges from 26.4% to 92.7%, but under differential fuzzing only 31.4% of all generated function bodies that compile, pooled over models and samples, are equivalent to the original. Divergence at the contract level is the norm rather than the exception: for six of the seven models, between 13% and 31% of the generated contracts that compile diverge from the original under historical replay, and between 13% and 44% under DCR-guided replay; only Gemma-4-31B stays below 3% on both. Compilation is therefore a necessary condition for correctness and far from a sufficient one.

Software Engineering.title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary:
The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.
  In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.
  We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.

Software Engineering.title: Designing Collaborative AI-Driven Workflows for Scientific Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems can carry out a broad range of tasks in software engineering and scientific research, from writing and translating code to running workflows for data analysis and visualization. In scientific computing, the difficulty is verifying that agent-generated code is both correct and understandable to teams whose members bring different areas of expertise. We therefore argue that these systems are best used within collaborative team structures rather than as full automation. In the workflows we propose, domain experts write the specification and plan, and agents operate under a deterministic orchestration pattern to write the target code. Each stage ends with a numerical comparison against the reference code and requires human review and approval before the next begins. We evaluate these workflows on the translation of a large high-energy physics application from Fortran to C++, running the same task under different orchestrators, design patterns, and models. Across fourteen experiments, a simple author--reviewer loop with enforced limits completed a comparable number of files to a multi-agent workflow at about one-third of the cost per file.

Software Engineering.title: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
Software Engineering.summary: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node.js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X.js, a live benchmark of real-world Node.js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X.js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X.js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X.js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node.js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.

Software Engineering.title: Towards a Taxonomy of Software Log Smells
Software Engineering.summary: Logging is an important part of modern software projects; logs are used in several tasks such as debugging and testing. Due to the complex nature of logging, it remains a difficult task with several pitfalls that could have serious consequences. Several other domains of software engineering have mitigated such threats by identifying the early signs of more serious issues, i.e., ``smells''. However, in the context of software logging, the concept of smells has only been investigated in a limited and narrow scope. The goal of this study is to systematically organize logging issues reported in the literature into a taxonomy of log smells that can help practitioners to better understand logging quality issues. To further help the practitioners and to identify issues that need more attention from the research community, we also map the identified smells to existing tools repairing them. We conducted a survey of the scientific literature to identify logging issues and related tools. After extracting relevant data from 61 articles, we used open coding to define logging issues and applied card sorting to derive log smells from these issues. Finally, we classified the tools based on their reported output. We present a taxonomy of nine log smells, describe several facets for each of them, and report the results of a preliminary validation of the taxonomy using a dataset of logging issues extracted from open-source projects. We also review existing tools repairing/removing some of these facets, highlighting the lack of tools addressing some log smells and identifying future research opportunities to close this gap. Our findings indicate that software logging is susceptible to a wide variety of log smells affecting both the logging code and the resulting log files. Understanding these smells, along with their causes and consequences, can help reduce their occurrence and improve logging quality.
Software Engineering.comment: 43 pages, 4 figures. We added a second reviewer for the literature survey and a preliminary validation

Software Engineering.title: APTree: Extended Behavior Trees for Adaptive and Scalable Automated Robotic Task Planning in Construction
Software Engineering.summary: Task planning for robots in off-site construction prefabrication is primarily manual, leading to planning inefficiencies and reluctance to adopt robotic solutions. Existing approaches provide limited support for scalable, modular automated task planning and localized runtime replanning. This paper proposes APTree, a model-driven framework that integrates automated task planning with modular task execution using behavior trees as the execution model. APTree repeatedly applies and coordinates heterogeneous symbolic planners to automatically generate and compose modular task plans at runtime. To support this approach, we develop a domain-specific language for the formal specification and validation of task plans, together with a compatible execution engine. We evaluate APTree on the real-world livMatS Biomimetic Shell pavilion, where it models the construction robotic fabrication domain, detects injected specification and planning errors at design time and runtime, and automatically generates large-scale task plans by coordinating three symbolic planners across numerous planning modules. A machine-checked formal analysis further shows that composed execution and local replanning are safe under explicitly stated assumptions, including planner soundness and non-interference of generated plans, providing practitioners with explicit conditions for dependable plan composition. APTree thus enables construction practitioners to leverage automated task planning without requiring detailed knowledge of symbolic planning techniques or APTree's internal implementation.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication in The Journal of Systems and Software. 46 pages, 17 figures, 16 listings, 6 tables

Software Engineering.title: Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Fine-Tuning in Code-Related Tasks
Software Engineering.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have proven highly effective in automating software engineering tasks, bridging natural language and code semantics to achieve notable results in code generation and summarization. However, their scale incurs substantial computational costs, making full fine-tuning impractical. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like QLoRA enable efficient specialization with lower resource demands. Recent studies show QLoRA-optimized Large Code Models (LCMs) perform strongly across diverse tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this effectiveness persists when a single model is QLoRA fine-tuned for multiple code-related tasks. The interaction between Multi-task fine-tuning and QLoRA optimization, and how transfer learning affects correctness and quality of generated artifacts, remains largely unexplored. We investigate Multi-task QLoRA fine-tuning --- a representative parameter-efficient method from the LoRA family --- across three representative tasks: code generation, translation, and summarization. We evaluate functional correctness through execution-based and similarity-based metrics, complemented by comprehensive code quality analysis--an aspect largely overlooked in prior work. Our findings show that Multi-task QLoRA effectively leverages transfer learning, achieving competitive or superior performance at the 1.5B, 3B, and 7B configurations relative to both Single-task QLoRA and Multi-task full fine-tuning. Larger models demonstrate more consistent balance between correctness and quality, whereas smaller models preserve functionality but exhibit a higher incidence of quality-related issues.

Software Engineering.title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Terminal agents have shown strong abilities in complex coding tasks. However, they often struggle to recover from errors during long-running execution (e.g., command errors, faulty implementations), eventually leading to task failures. To this end, we present ReTerm, a self-improving terminal agent trained by learning how to recover from its own failed terminal tasks. To support its training, we construct a customized data pipeline and produce ReTerm-10K, a high-quality dataset that provides effective recovery demonstrations for SFT cold start. Furthermore, we propose ReTerm-GRPO, an online RL algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate multiple independent self-recovery attempts. By learning from whether these attempts successfully complete the task, the agent self-improves through its own recovery experience. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, our ReTerm-9B achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, improving over the base model by 14.6 points. Further analysis shows that our method achieves consistently higher recovery rates across diverse error categories compared with standard GRPO training. All code, data and model are released at https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm.

Software Engineering.title: OctoLong: Mid-Training On Cross-Repository Code Contexts Enhances Long-Context Modeling
Software Engineering.summary: Context lengths of language models (LMs) have dramatically increased, driven by the demands for in-context learning, self-improvement, and long-horizon agentic workflows. However, existing long-context corpora are dominated by books, academic articles, and code repositories, which are finite and often lack long-distance dependencies. In this work, we introduce OctoLong, a context-engineering pipeline that instruments an AST parser, a language server backend, and a package manager to recursively retrieve code references, enabling the curation of dependency-rich code contexts up to millions of tokens long. We then train OctoLong-Instruct, a suite of capable long-context open LMs, derived from base models ranging in size from 600M to 14B parameters, via context-extension mid-training on a approx 50B-token mixture containing approx 6.2B tokens of OctoLong code contexts, followed by approx 10B tokens of instruction tuning. Our ablations and experimental evaluations against 18 strong long-context open-weight LMs show that supplanting just 12% of conventional context-extension corpora with OctoLong data yields substantial gains in long-range retrieval, long-term state tracking, repository-level code understanding, and downstream agentic tasks, while also enhancing API usage in regular coding scenarios.

Software Engineering.title: REINS: Agent-guided Thread Scheduling for Concurrency Bug Detection and Reproduction
Software Engineering.summary: Concurrency bugs manifest only under specific thread interleavings, making them hard to detect and reproduce. Existing controlled concurrency testing techniques take over thread scheduling to explore the interleaving space. As the space grows rapidly with program scale, finding interleavings that can trigger bugs within a limited budget remains challenging. The program's concurrency semantics can reveal which variable accesses and synchronization operations under specific interleavings lead to unexpected program behavior, and thus help focus the exploration on bug-relevant interleavings. However, prior techniques have not fully exploited such semantic information. In this paper, we present REINS, an agentic approach for detecting and reproducing concurrency bugs. At its core, REINS guides thread scheduling with the agent's reasoning about the concurrency semantics and known concurrency bug patterns. REINS starts with runtime observations and combines them with static information to reason about the program's concurrency behavior and formulate hypotheses about potential bugs. A hypothesis translates into a set of constraints on event orders and variable states, guiding a controlled scheduler toward interleavings likely to trigger the bug. REINS draws conclusions from the execution results and keeps refining the constraints until the bug is triggered or the hypothesis is refuted. Compared with existing techniques on three public benchmarks, REINS detects more bugs within the same time budget. Furthermore, REINS found six previously unknown concurrency bugs in real-world projects, three of which have been confirmed by the developers.

Software Engineering.title: Developer Experience with AI Coding Agents: HTTP Behavioral Signatures in Documentation Portals
Software Engineering.summary: The rapid adoption of AI coding agents and AI assistant web services is fundamentally changing how developers discover, consume, and interact with technical documentation. This paper studies that transformation across three interconnected dimensions: documentation accessibility, content analytics, and feedback systems. We present an empirical study of HTTP request fingerprints from nine AI coding agents (Aider, Antigravity, Claude Code, Cline, Cursor, Junie, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot (VS Code agent mode), and Windsurf) and six AI assistant services (ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini, Google NotebookLM, MistralAI, and Perplexity) accessing a live developer documentation endpoint, revealing identifiable behavioral signatures in HTTP runtime environments, pre-fetch strategies, User-Agent strings, and header patterns. Our study shows that AI agent access compresses multi-page navigation into a single or two requests, making traditional engagement metrics - session depth, time-on-page, click path, and bounce rate - unreliable indicators of actual documentation consumption. We discuss practical adaptations for developer portal teams, including tokenomics-aware documentation design, adoption of emerging machine-readable standards (AGENTS.md, llms.txt, skill.md, agent-permissions.json), MCP server-based feedback channels, and analytics instrumentation for AI referral traffic.
Software Engineering.comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Extended version. A 2-page extended abstract, "Documentation Retrieval by AI Coding Agents: An Empirical Study of HTTP Behavioral Signatures", appears in AgenticDev '26 (ASE 2026 workshop), DOI: 10.1145/3843282.3844445. Please cite the ACM version

Software Engineering.title: SWE-MISBEHAVIOR: Benchmarking and Mitigating Boundary Violations in Software Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: We present SWE-MISBEHAVIOR, the first taxonomy and evaluation framework for diagnosing boundary-violating misbehaviors in coding agents. It contains 7.4K human-in-the-loop synthesized samples spanning three layers of agent action space: (i) Code Generation, (ii) File Management, and (iii) System Interaction. Across these categories, SWE-MISBEHAVIOR covers 11 distinct misbehaviors with a fully automated evaluation protocol, including coding-action violations, Create/Read/Update/Delete (CRUD) file misbehaviors, system integrity and abuse violations, and task-goal misalignment. Experiments on state-of-the-art open-source coding agents (e.g., OpenHands, smolagents) reveal substantial misaligned behaviors, including dependency misinterpretation (up to 98.5% of cases), unintended modification of user inputs (50.5%), and silent compromise of environment integrity (53%). Motivated by these findings, we further propose CODE-KIT, a lightweight adaptive framework that combines misbehavior-aware guidelines with novel tools to help agents avoid such failures. CODE-KIT reduces misbehaviors by 52% for smolagents and 34% for OpenHands, while simultaneously improving task completion performance.
Software Engineering.comment: Codes and data are available at https://github.com/dxlong2000/SWE-Misbehavior

Software Engineering.title: Assessing the Quality of Concrete Scenarios Generated from Scenario Classes for Automated Driving
Software Engineering.summary: A scenario-based development approach has become state of the art for automated driving systems. Once a set of scenario classes covering the operational design domain is available, concrete scenarios are generated from these scenario classes, e.g., to be used for hazard analysis and risk assessment or for the system's verification and validation. For such applications, a high diversity among the generated concrete scenarios is paramount. The question arises how the quality of collections of concrete scenarios can be assessed in such a setting. In this work, we aggregate scenario distance measures into so-called quality functions that quantify the diversity of concrete scenario collections in the context of automated driving. In particular, we consider the case where scenario classes are formalized as constraint systems and the associated concrete scenario space is not explicitly known. Based on a set of desired properties we construct candidates for such quality functions and give proofs for their property fulfillment. To show the practical relevance of quality functions, we perform a variety of experiments in the context of an abstract scenario-based virtual verification toolchain for automated driving systems. More specifically, we use quality functions to compare the effectiveness of variation methods for sampling, examine the choice of different scenario distance measures, and investigate the effects of temporal aspects on concrete scenario collection quality.

Software Engineering.title: Soliduzz: Finding Miscompilations in Smart-Contract Compilers with Assertion-Driven Equivalence Oracles
Software Engineering.summary:
Smart contracts compiled to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) can manage high-value assets and are difficult to patch after deployment. Compiler miscompilations are therefore especially dangerous: compilation succeeds, but the generated bytecode does not preserve the semantics of the source program. Existing smart-contract compiler fuzzers either focus on robustness failures or rely on differential oracles that compare compiler configurations.
  We present Soliduzz, an approach for finding miscompilations in EVM smart-contract compilers using assertion-driven equivalence oracles. Soliduzz uses product programs to encode semantic equivalence as executable assertions. The key shift is to compile these self-checking programs and let off-the-shelf fuzzers and symbolic execution engines explore the resulting bytecode for assertion violations, without requiring compiler-specific support from the analyzer.
  Soliduzz instantiates this idea with two complementary families of metamorphic transformations. The first starts from equivalent expressions and lifts them into smart-contract code that deliberately exercises EVM-specific features such as storage, data locations, control flow, contract interactions, and inline assembly. The second generalizes Equivalence Modulo Inputs (EMI) from fixed concrete inputs to symbolic input spaces. Our symbolic EMI records coverage in the original computation and uses it to guard mutations in the transformed computation. Together, these transformations produce product programs that assert that paired computations yield the same outputs.
  We evaluate Soliduzz on three EVM smart-contract compilers (solc, solx, and vyper) using several analysis tools. Overall, Soliduzz exposes 29 bugs. Of these, 24 are compiler bugs: 6 miscompilations, 17 internal compiler errors, and 1 hang. The remaining 5 are bugs in the analysis tools.

Software Engineering.title: yProv4DV: Filling the visualization gap in reproducible research workflows
Software Engineering.summary: While results visualization is a critical phase to the communication of new academic results, plots are frequently shared without the complete combination of code, input data, execution context and outputs required to independently reproduce the resulting figures. Existing reproducibility solutions tend to focus on computational pipelines or workflow management systems, not covering script-based visualization practices commonly used by researchers and practitioners. Additionally, the minimalist nature of current Python data visualization libraries tend to speed up the creation of images, disincentivizing users from spending time integrating additional tools into these short scripts. This paper proposes yProv4DV, a library lightweight designed to enable reproducible data visualization scripts through the use of provenance information, minimizing the necessity for code modifications. Through a single call, users can track inputs, outputs and source code files, enabling saving and full reproducibility of their data visualization software. As a result, this library fills a gap in reproducible research workflows by addressing the reproducibility of plots in scientific publications.

Software Engineering.title: SWEPatchTest: Evaluating Software Tests Beyond Reproduction
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents use generated tests to decide whether a proposed patch satisfies an issue's requirements. A suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after applying the reference patch can still accept an incorrect patch or reject a correct patch. We introduce SWEPATCHTEST, a test-generation benchmark with 619 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual, and DeepSWE and 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories. By replaying each suite on the buggy and patched codebases, \benchmark jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect patches. Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three criteria on the same task, exposes failures hidden by single-reference evaluation: the best-performing configuration achieves only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks. We further use validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The resulting training recipe approximately triples JVR and improves downstream repair across three SWE-bench benchmarks. Patch discrimination thus provides both a diagnostic measure of test quality and an execution-based signal for curating agent training data.

Software Engineering.title: From Rocq to Metal: A Pipeline for Formally Verified Microcontroller Firmware
Software Engineering.summary: Enforcing invariants in safety-critical firmware is increasingly urgent as generated code becomes widespread, but standard extraction targets for proof assistants require runtimes too large for many embedded devices. We present a pipeline for running formally verified Rocq firmware logic on Cortex-M microcontrollers. The pipeline extracts Gallina to Scheme, compiles it with Encore!, a bare-metal Continuation-Passing Style (CPS) bytecode virtual machine, and embeds the result in no_std Rust firmware. We structure applications as pure state-transition functions, so the business logic is proved in Rocq while the event/effect boundary, host callbacks, compiler, and VM remain explicit trusted components: no proof yet relates bytecode execution to Gallina semantics. On eight firmware workloads, from APDU parsing to a credential store, Encore! runs unmodified Rocq-extracted code within the 50 KiB RAM budget of ST33-class targets on every input size, where CertiRocq's generated code runs out of memory on the larger ones, at the price of up to 10 times more executed instructions than CertiRocq; a transaction-signing application is validated on physical Ledger Flex hardware.
Software Engineering.comment: Preprint: Accepted to the 19th International Conference on Verification and Evaluation of Computer and Communication Systems (VECoS 2026)

Software Engineering.title: Stdlib or Third-Party? Empirical Performance and Correctness of LLM-Assisted Zero-Dependency Python Libraries
Software Engineering.summary:
Third-party Python libraries introduce dependency-management overhead, supply-chain risk, and deployment friction. We study when eliminating a dependency preserves enough correctness and performance to justify the gains in footprint, deployability, and trust surface. Our testbed is zerodep, 44 single-file, stdlib-only Python modules spanning 12 categories, each benchmarked against its reference library.
  Three performance regimes emerge. Stdlib-only implementations achieve parity (within 2x) in the majority of cases; many outperform their references by 5x-115x where architectural overhead dominates; and a clear cliff appears for C-extension-backed computation (image processing, binary serialization, low-level crypto), confirmed by PyPy JIT and profiling experiments. Beyond speed, stdlib modules reduce installed footprint by orders of magnitude (median 31 KB vs. 700 KB), import 2.2x faster, and eliminate 88 transitive dependencies maintained by 128 distinct PyPI accounts.
  Analysis of the LLM-assisted development process across all 44 modules shows that specification completeness, not model capability, is a strong predictor of generation success, and that contract-linked review reduces review volume by 5x while eliminating compatibility regressions. Together, these results turn dependency elimination from an anecdotal coding style into an evidence-based engineering tradeoff.

Software Engineering.title: Porting Declarative UI to HarmonyOS: A Heuristic-guided Approach for lightweight LLMs
Software Engineering.summary:
As an emerging operating system, HarmonyOS has a significant demand for software migration, where the User Interface (UI) translation accounts for a critical link. However, recent UI development has shifted to declarative paradigms, e.g., Kotlin Jetpack Compose (KJC) for Android, SwiftUI for iOS, and ArkUI for HarmonyOS, making prior translation approaches inapplicable because they target either backend logic or legacy imperative UIs. Thus, related research is limited.
  To systematically evaluate KJC/SwiftUI-to-ArkUI migration, we build a parallel benchmark of 100 KJC and 100 SwiftUI files across eight scenarios, plus 52 real-world UI pages from nine open-source apps. Evaluating nine direct-translation setups (including diverse LLMs and agents), we find Compilation Success Rate (CSR) spans 0.00%-35.00%; common strategies (reference screenshots and compiler-guided repair) lift capable setups to 94.00%-99.00% CSR but fail on lightweight LLMs. By manually analyzing a 3,102-sample subset, deriving a regular-expression pattern for each failure family, and applying these patterns to generalize the resulting taxonomy to the full 29,593-sample set, we find residual errors rooted in (1) broken structure, (2) nonexistent APIs, and (3) missing resources (e.g., colors, strings, and icons).
  Accordingly, we propose ArkTrans, a declarative UI translation framework that maps these roots to deterministic structure supply, ArkUI knowledge and resource reference injection via a demonstration example, and iterative repair targeting residual errors, via four steps: Metadata Extraction, Skeleton Construction, LLM-driven Translation, and Compiler-Guided Iterative Repair. With Qwen3.6-27B, ArkTrans raises CSR from 0.00% to 70.00% on KJC and 64.00% on SwiftUI, achieving strong visual fidelity, and attains 65.63%/80.00% CSR on real-world pages, far outperforming the best common strategy at lower token cost.

Software Engineering.title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
Software Engineering.summary: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.

Software Engineering.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both \emph{evaluation} and \emph{generation} of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

Software Engineering.title: Mobile App Analysis in the New Era: Challenges and the Road Ahead
Software Engineering.summary: Mobile applications (apps) have grown into complex, multi-platform systems that support diverse services and operate within varying regulatory and distribution contexts. Traditional analysis techniques have established a strong foundation for ensuring quality, security, and compliance, but face increasing challenges as mobile apps evolve. This article presents a three-layer perspective to examine these challenges. The Artifact Layer highlights how heterogeneous code bases and protection mechanisms reduce the analyzability of packaged apps. The Runtime Layer addresses growing execution complexity, from multi-modal interactions and super-app architectures to AI-driven autonomous operations. The Ecosystem Layer considers broader contexts, including emerging platforms, fragmented distribution channels, and region-specific regulatory requirements.
